title: How the Alberta government could fill a new pipeline with royalties paid in oil
summary: To overcome one of the biggest challenges facing Premier Danielle Smith’s ambitions to build a large oil export pipeline to the West Coast, the Alberta government could decide to fill the pipeline…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith attends the Oil Sands Expo in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Sept. 16. The Alberta government is looking for oil producers to sign long-term contracts to ship on the proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis

To overcome one of the biggest challenges facing Premier Danielle Smith’s ambitions to build a large oil export pipeline to the West Coast, the Alberta government could decide to fill the pipeline with oil collected as royalties from industry.
Royalties-in-kind mean province can collect oil instead of cash — then use it to ensure pipeline goes ahead

One of the biggest challenges facing Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s ambitions to develop and build a large oil export pipeline to the West Coast is having oil companies sign long-term contracts to actually use the proposed project.

If that hurdle becomes too big to overcome, the Alberta government could turn to a relatively unknown policy that allows the energy royalties it receives to be paid in oil — and then use that oil to service the pipeline.

Companies have to pay a royalty to the provincial government for any oil and natural gas produced in Alberta. These monthly royalties add billions of dollars in revenue to provincial coffers each year.

But some industry experts say the provincial government could instead use the "royalty-in-kind" policy to collect enough oil to fill the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, which would transport oil from the Edmonton area to a port near Vancouver.

blocks.text: "If there needs to be more barrels that are diverted and are sent on the Pacific Link when constructed, for sure the Crown could elect to take more and more of its royalty in bitumen and physically allocate it to the Pacific Link," said Grant Sprague, a former deputy energy minister in Alberta.

For now, Smith is focused on encouraging the largest oil companies in the province to ramp up oil production, which is why the premier unveiled a new incentive program last week focused on promoting the construction of new oilsands facilities.
A view of Suncor's Base Plant oilsands mine. Suncor is one of the companies considering whether to proceed with expanding production in the oilsands. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)
More production is the ideal way of filling the Pacific Link pipeline, said Sprague, since the royalty-in-kind program would not help Alberta’s overall goal of increasing oil exports.
"It's a diversion. It's never additive. And I think the real goal has got to be to have sufficient production to fill — maybe not fill, but to service all of the existing pipelines," said Sprague.
"… Short answer: it's not a panacea."
Financial repercussions
Requiring companies to pay royalties in oil could also come at a financial cost for producers.

Oil companies have long-term contracts on other export pipelines to ship a certain amount of oil. If a producer would not have as much oil to fill their space on the pipelines, they would still have to pay for the amount of pipeline capacity they are signed up for.
That would result in oil producers paying for shipping on "air barrels."

Former Suncor chief executive Mark Little said he's "very certain" the Alberta government is considering the option to take payment in barrels of oil — and companies would feel the squeeze if it went ahead.
"It's a hit on the company's financial performance unless they expand," Little said.
"I think we're going to see some capital get invested just because they're either going to go willingly or get somewhat forced."

Alberta could access enough oil to fill the million-barrels-per-day Pacific Link pipeline by using the royalties-in-kind program, said a government official, speaking on background. However, the official said, it is not the government’s intent to do so, since it is confident the oilpatch will increase production.

blocks.text: The Pacific Link project faces other challenges, including legal challenges filed by three First Nations in Alberta in an attempt to overturn the federal government’s designation of the pipeline as a project in the national interest.
The designation allows the federal government to fast-track and consolidate the approval process for the pipeline under the Building Canada Act.
'If they want to acquire some barrels, just go buy them'

Foregoing royalty payments in cash could also blow a hole in Alberta's budget. Other ramifications include souring the investment climate at a time when Alberta is trying to attract tens of billions of dollars to grow its energy sector and double oil production.

"If you're trying to attract new investment to increase growth, threatening people ain't the way to do it," said Richard Masson, former chief executive of the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission, the province’s commercial oil and gas agency that runs the royalty-in-kind program.
"Royalties-in-kind is just a mechanism that complicates life, creates uncertainty and doesn't create an extra barrel to ship," he said.
Richard Masson, former chief executive of the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission, does not think using the royalty-in-kind program is a good idea for the province. (Justin Pennell/CBC)
If the provincial government needs oil to fill its pipeline, it’s much easier to purchase barrels on the open market, he said.
"Alberta gets its royalties in cash every month at the market price. If they want to acquire some barrels, just go buy them," said Masson. "Easy-peasy."

The Alberta government has said one of the reasons for having the royalties-in-kind program is to have "more control over the province’s resources, allowing for the expansion of egress and market access."

Some large oilpatch companies have been reluctant to build new oil production facilities because of a lack of support from shareholders. Despite lucrative oil prices, many investors would rather oil companies continue to produce hefty profits, as opposed to spending billions of dollars to invest in new projects.

blocks.text: The chances of the provincial government using the policy are relatively small, considering the financial harm it could cause some oil companies — but it does provide a pathway for the proposed pipeline to proceed even if oil companies don’t sign contracts committing to use it.

At the same time, the policy gives the provincial government an important tool to motivate the oilpatch to invest in pumping out more crude, even though it would complicate its relationship with Alberta's largest industry.
"There's this really interesting tension that I've never seen before," said Little, the former Suncor CEO.
